reviews.scope: proving lines parallel inside combined arguments
reviews.reason: Combined reasoning must decide when to use a criterion and then apply corresponding, alternate or co-interior angle conditions to conclude parallelism. That criterion knowledge cannot be bypassed.

reviews.scope: deriving angle relations from known parallels
reviews.reason: Bent-line angle models and auxiliary parallel constructions depend on transferring equal or supplementary angles from parallel lines. This is exactly the properties content, so no alternative route exists.

Parallel line properties give clean conditional statements for practicing condition and conclusion. However, the logic of propositions, truth and counterexamples can be taught with any mathematical statements.
reviews.counterexample: Use number statements such as 'if a>b then a+c>b+c' as the examples.

reviews.scope: intuitive notion of sliding a figure
reviews.reason: The primary-school intuition of sliding by grid squares eases the transition. The formal node, however, defines translation and its properties completely, so it can be learned without that earlier experience.
reviews.counterexample: A learner meets translation first through the formal direction-and-distance definition.

reviews.reason: The stated property says segments joining corresponding points are parallel or collinear. Understanding and checking that property needs the concept of parallel lines in a plane.
Constructing an image means moving every vertex the same direction and distance while preserving shape. That procedure is the direct application of the translation definition and its properties.

reviews.scope: definition via x squared and sign facts
reviews.reason: A square root is defined by x squared equal to a. Seeing that positives have two opposite roots and negatives have none relies on even-power sign rules.

reviews.scope: computing roots and simplifying sqrt(a squared)
reviews.reason: Finding roots of perfect squares and knowing that sqrt(a squared) equals |a| both presuppose what a square root and a principal root are, along with their notation.

reviews.scope: contrasting cube roots with square roots
reviews.reason: Cube roots can be defined independently. The explicit criterion, though, asks students to state how cube roots differ from square roots, which requires prior square root knowledge.

Classifying numbers such as sqrt4 versus sqrt2 needs the ability to evaluate perfect square roots. Without that, students cannot tell which radicals are rational. Decimal and pi cases alone fall short of the criterion.

reviews.scope: classifying reals as rational or irrational
reviews.reason: Real numbers are defined as the union of rationals and irrationals. Classifying them and understanding why the number line is complete both depend on the irrational number concept.
The squeeze method places sqrt5 between sqrt4=2 and sqrt9=3. This uses known roots of perfect squares, which is exactly what this prerequisite covers.
Comparing values such as -sqrt5 and -2.2, or squared values, requires the rational ordering rules. This is especially true for negatives, where a larger absolute value means a smaller number.

reviews.scope: stating refined estimates to given accuracy
reviews.reason: Rounding conventions help when estimates are refined to tenths. Bracketing between integers and comparing sizes, however, need no knowledge of significant figures.
reviews.counterexample: Estimate sqrt7 as between 2 and 3 without any rounding.

reviews.scope: extending laws and absolute value to reals
reviews.reason: The node asserts that rational laws carry over to the real number system and uses opposites and absolute values of radicals. Both need the real number concept as a whole.

reviews.scope: order of operations in real expressions
reviews.reason: Real-number computation explicitly reuses rational operation rules. Mixed expressions with powers, parentheses and radicals cannot be evaluated correctly without the established order of operations.
Cube roots are common items in real-number computation exercises. Mastery of extending the operation rules can still be shown with square roots and pi alone, so only cube-root items depend on it.
reviews.counterexample: Compute 2sqrt3 - sqrt3 + |1 - sqrt2| with no cube roots.

reviews.scope: prior experience locating by column and row
reviews.reason: Primary grid work with number pairs builds the same intuition. The secondary node reteaches ordered pairs fully, including why order matters, so earlier mastery is helpful but not necessary.
reviews.counterexample: A learner first meets ordered pairs through seat or map positions in grade 7.

reviews.reason: A coordinate is an ordered pair in which swapping the entries changes the point. Plotting and writing coordinates relies directly on that ordered-pair idea.

reviews.scope: axes as number lines with negatives
reviews.reason: Each axis is a number line. Plotting points with negative or fractional coordinates requires locating and reading such numbers on a number line.
Formal perpendicular-line knowledge enriches the definition of the axes. Plotting and reading points needs only an informal right-angle idea, not perpendicular constructions or uniqueness.
reviews.counterexample: Use a printed grid with axes at a right angle without studying perpendicular lines.

reviews.scope: quadrant signs and points on axes
reviews.reason: Quadrants and axis-point features are properties of the coordinate system itself. Students cannot discuss sign patterns before they can locate points by coordinates.

reviews.scope: segment lengths and areas from coordinates
reviews.reason: Axis and quadrant features help organize distance-to-axis reasoning. Segment lengths, however, come from coordinate differences, and the real prerequisite is reading coordinates in the Cartesian Coordinate System and Point Coordinates node.
reviews.counterexample: Subtract the x-coordinates of two points with equal y without classifying quadrants.

reviews.reason: The absolute value of a coordinate difference is one formula for length. Ordering the coordinates and subtracting smaller from larger, or counting grid units, gives the same length.
reviews.counterexample: Compute 3-(-2)=5 by subtracting the smaller from the larger.

reviews.scope: setting up axes and recording locations
reviews.reason: Representing map locations means choosing an origin and unit and then writing point coordinates. That is an applied use of the coordinate system and cannot bypass it.
Coordinate rules for translation add or subtract values from x and y. Students must already read and write point coordinates to apply or reverse these rules.

reviews.scope: meaning of direction, distance, vertex-wise movement
reviews.reason: Coordinate rules encode translation direction and distance. The principle that a figure translates by moving every vertex identically comes from the translation concept and its properties.
Core tasks shift points by integer or rational units and need only rational addition. Irrational shifts are uncommon extensions, so this reflects chapter order rather than a meaningful dependency.
reviews.counterexample: Translate (2,-1) right 3 and up 4 using only integer arithmetic.

reviews.reason: The definition parallels the one-unknown case and is customarily taught by analogy. It can be stated directly from equation, unknown and term-degree ideas. The necessary base is Equations and Their Solutions.
reviews.counterexample: Define 'two unknowns, each of degree one, polynomial sides' directly.

reviews.scope: systems built from two-variable linear equations
reviews.reason: A system's solution is the common solution of its component equations. Checking a candidate pair requires knowing what solves a single two-variable linear equation.
Substitution is a procedure for obtaining the common solution of a system. Its goal and its check are defined by the meaning of a system's solution.
After substitution, the learner must transpose, combine like terms and normalize a one-variable linear equation, then back-substitute. Every substitution solve needs these steps.
Substituting an expression such as y=5-x into 2y yields 2(5-x). Expanding with the distributive and sign rules is unavoidable in general cases, even though trivial instances exist.

reviews.scope: meaning of the system being solved
reviews.reason: Adding or subtracting equations is justified because the pair satisfies both equations at once. Understanding the system and its common solution therefore underlies this method.
Elimination leaves a one-variable linear equation, and back-substitution gives forms like 3+2y=7. Both need transposition and coefficient normalization.
Substitution first introduces the idea of reducing two unknowns to one. Addition-subtraction elimination is justified independently by equality properties and can be learned first.
reviews.counterexample: Teach adding equations to cancel y before any substitution.

reviews.reason: A modeled system needs some valid solving method. Substitution is only one option, so addition-subtraction elimination fully suffices.
reviews.counterexample: Solve every modeled system by adding or subtracting equations.

reviews.reason: Addition-subtraction elimination is one interchangeable solving route. Students can solve all modeled systems by substitution instead.
reviews.counterexample: Solve every modeled system by substitution.

reviews.scope: general modeling workflow for word problems
reviews.reason: The one-unknown modeling sequence is customary preparation and transfers by analogy. Finding two equal relations and writing a system can, however, be taught directly.
reviews.counterexample: Introduce modeling with two unknowns from the start, then specialize.

reviews.reason: Classifying problem types and finding their equal relations builds on the general skill of setting two unknowns, writing a system and checking solutions.
Meeting and catch-up analysis supplies familiar distance relations. Only one problem type benefits, and distance equals speed times time can be applied directly with two unknowns.
reviews.counterexample: Model a two-speed travel problem from d=vt without prior one-variable travel work.

reviews.reason: Earlier cost comparison and break-even reasoning helps with plan problems. These remain one category among many, and they can be modeled directly with systems.
reviews.counterexample: Solve a distribution plan system without prior piecewise pricing study.

reviews.reason: Reducing a three-variable system requires some elimination technique. Substitution is one route, and addition-subtraction elimination alone can complete every reduction.
reviews.counterexample: Eliminate z from two pairs by adding equations, then solve the 2x2 system the same way.

reviews.reason: Addition-subtraction elimination is a common choice but not the only one. Successive substitution also reduces the system to two unknowns and then to one.
reviews.counterexample: Express z from one equation and substitute into the other two.

reviews.reason: Inequalities state order relations among rational quantities. Checking whether a value is a solution means comparing numbers, including negatives, correctly.

reviews.scope: meaning of a solution by analogy
reviews.reason: Equation solutions give a model for an inequality solution. The idea of a value making an inequality true, and of the set of all such values, can be taught directly.
reviews.counterexample: Test values in x>2 and collect all that work without equation background.

reviews.reason: Graphing a solution set, with open or closed endpoints, presupposes knowing what a solution set is and whether the boundary value is included.
The properties describe operations that keep an inequality true. Their meaning depends on understanding an inequality and its order relation.

reviews.scope: multiplying or dividing by negative numbers
reviews.reason: Applying the reversal rule requires computing products and quotients with negative factors. Its justification also rests on how multiplying by a negative reverses order.
Equality properties give a parallel template that highlights the new direction change. The inequality properties stand on order facts and can be learned directly.
reviews.counterexample: Derive the properties from number-line examples without prior equality work.

reviews.reason: Each step, especially dividing by a negative coefficient, is valid only by the inequality properties. Without them, students cannot avoid errors in the sign direction.
The explicit criterion asks students to show the solution set on a number line. That requires the open and closed endpoint representation skill.

Equation solving with denominators is the customary template, and its LCM step transfers. Each step can instead be derived directly from inequality properties, and many inequalities have no fractions.
reviews.counterexample: Multiply x/2 - 1 > x/3 by 6 justified only by the positive-multiplier property.

reviews.reason: Finding integer solutions or optimal plans requires solving the set-up linear inequality, including reversing the sign when dividing by negatives, before interpreting results.
The equation modeling routine transfers by analogy. Translating phrases like 'at least' into inequalities and choosing integer answers can, however, be taught directly.
reviews.counterexample: Teach inequality word problems from verbal translation without equation modeling practice.
